claim: Humans somatically generate highly diverse repertoires of B cell and T cell receptors (BCRs and TCRs) through a random process called V(D)J recombination.
source: To appropriately defend against a wide array of pathogens, humans somatically generate highly diverse repertoires of B cell and T cell receptors (BCRs and TCRs) through a random process called V(D)J recombination.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the adaptive immune system and is stated as background information in the abstract.

claim: Receptor diversity is achieved during V(D)J recombination through both the combinatorial assembly of V(D)J-genes and the junctional deletion and insertion of nucleotides.
source: Receptor diversity is achieved during this process through both the combinatorial assembly of V(D)J-genes and the junctional deletion and insertion of nucleotides.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about V(D)J recombination mechanisms stated in the abstract.

claim: The Artemis protein is often regarded as the main nuclease involved in V(D)J recombination.
source: While the Artemis protein is often regarded as the main nuclease involved in V(D)J recombination, the exact mechanism of nucleotide trimming is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, though the authors note the mechanism is not fully understood.

claim: The exact mechanism of nucleotide trimming during V(D)J recombination is not understood.
source: While the Artemis protein is often regarded as the main nuclease involved in V(D)J recombination, the exact mechanism of nucleotide trimming is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Local sequence context, length, and GC nucleotide content in both directions of the wider sequence, together, can most accurately predict the trimming probabilities of a given V-gene sequence.
source: We show that local sequence context, length, and GC nucleotide content in both directions of the wider sequence, together, can most accurately predict the trimming probabilities of a given V-gene sequence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the modeling results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GC nucleotide content is predictive of sequence-breathing.
source: Because GC nucleotide content is predictive of sequence-breathing, this model provides quantitative statistical evidence regarding the extent to which double-stranded DNA may need to be able to breathe for trimming to occur.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DNA structure and dynamics.

claim: The model provides quantitative statistical evidence regarding the extent to which double-stranded DNA may need to be able to breathe for trimming to occur.
source: Because GC nucleotide content is predictive of sequence-breathing, this model provides quantitative statistical evidence regarding the extent to which double-stranded DNA may need to be able to breathe for trimming to occur.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the modeling results and interpretation of GC content effects.

claim: There is evidence of a sequence motif that appears to get preferentially trimmed, independent of GC-content-related effects.
source: We also see evidence of a sequence motif that appears to get preferentially trimmed, independent of GC-content-related effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the motif analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The inferred coefficients from the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model provide accurate prediction for V- and J-gene sequences from other adaptive immune receptor loci.
source: Further, we find that the inferred coefficients from this model provide accurate prediction for V- and J-gene sequences from other adaptive immune receptor loci.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The majority of human T cells express α-β receptors that consist of an α and a β protein chain.
source: The majority of human T cells express α-β receptors that consist of an α and a β protein chain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell receptor biology stated in the introduction.

claim: During V(D)J recombination of the β chain, a single V-, D-, and J-gene are randomly chosen from a pool of V-gene, D-gene, and J-gene segments within the germline TCRβ locus over a series of steps.
source: During the V(D)J recombination process of the β chain, a single V-, D-, and J-gene are randomly chosen from a pool of V-gene, D-gene, and J-gene segments within the germline TCRβ locus over a series of steps.
evidence: This is established knowledge about V(D)J recombination stated in the introduction.

claim: The recombination activating gene protein complex aligns a randomly chosen D- and J-gene, removes the intervening chromosomal DNA between the two genes, and forms a hairpin loop at the end of each gene.
source: To begin this process, the recombination activating gene protein complex aligns a randomly chosen D- and J-gene, removes the intervening chromosomal DNA between the two genes, and forms a hairpin loop at the end of each gene (Gellert, 1994; Fugmann et al., 2000; Schatz and Swanson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Each hairpin loop is nicked open, typically in an asymmetrical fashion, by the Artemis:DNA-PKcs protein complex.
source: Each hairpin loop is then nicked open, typically in an asymmetrical fashion, by the Artemis:DNA-PKcs protein complex (Ma et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Asymmetrical hairpin opening creates a single-stranded DNA overhang at the end of both genes that may contain P-nucleotides.
source: This asymmetrical hairpin opening creates a single-stranded DNA overhang at the end of both genes that, depending on the location of the hairpin nick, may contain P-nucleotides (short palindromes of gene terminal sequence) (Gauss and Lieber, 1996; Nadel and Feeney, 1997; Ma et al., 2002; Jackson et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The most dominant hairpin opening position leads to a single-stranded 3' overhang that is 4 nucleotides in length (2 nucleotides of which are P-nucleotides).
source: The most dominant hairpin opening position leads to a single-stranded 3' overhang that is 4 nucleotides in length (2 nucleotides of which are P-nucleotides) (Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nucleotides may be deleted from each gene end through an incompletely understood mechanism suggested to involve Artemis.
source: From here, nucleotides may be deleted from each gene end through an incompletely understood mechanism suggested to involve Artemis (Feeney et al., 1994; Nadel and Feeney, 1995; Nadel and Feeney, 1997; Jackson et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2015; Chang and Lieber, 2016; Zhao et al., 2020; Russell et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nucleotide trimming can remove traces of P-nucleotides.
source: This nucleotide trimming can remove traces of P-nucleotides (Gauss and Lieber, 1996; Srivastava and Robins, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Non-template-encoded nucleotides, known as N-insertions, can be added to each gene end by the enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.
source: Non-template-encoded nucleotides, known as N-insertions, can also be added to each gene end by the enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (Kallenbach et al., 1992; Gilfillan et al., 1993; Komori et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Small variations in gene sequence have been shown to lead to large changes in the extent of nucleotide deletion.
source: Small variations in gene sequence have been shown to lead to large changes in the extent of nucleotide deletion (Nadel and Feeney, 1995; Gauss and Lieber, 1996; Nadel and Feeney, 1997; Jackson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sequences with high AT content suffer greater nucleotide loss than sequences with high GC content.
source: For example, sequences with high AT content suffer greater nucleotide loss than sequences with high GC content (Gauss and Lieber, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Artemis possesses intrinsic 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity on single-stranded DNA.
source: Alone, Artemis possesses intrinsic 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity on single-stranded DNA (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: On double-stranded DNA, Artemis, in complex with DNA-PKcs, has endonuclease activity on 5' and 3' DNA overhangs and on DNA hairpins.
source: On double-stranded DNA, Artemis, in complex with DNA-PKcs, has endonuclease activity on 5' and 3' DNA overhangs and on DNA hairpins (Ma et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex binds single-stranded-to-double-stranded DNA boundaries prior to nicking.
source: It has been proposed that the Artemis:DNA-PKcs complex binds single-stranded-to-double-stranded DNA boundaries prior to nicking (Ma et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2007; Chang and Lieber, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For blunt DNA ends, sequence-breathing is required to achieve a structural configuration suitable for Artemis action.
source: for blunt DNA ends, previous work has concluded that sequence-breathing is required to achieve this structural configuration prior to Artemis action (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Artemis, in complex with XRCC4-DNA ligase IV, has additional endonuclease activity on 3' DNA overhangs and preferentially nicks one nucleotide at a time from the single-stranded 3' end.
source: Further, Artemis, in complex with XRCC4-DNA ligase IV, has additional endonuclease activity on 3' DNA overhangs and preferentially nicks one nucleotide at a time from the single-stranded 3' end (Chang et al., 2016; Gerodimos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A simple position-weight-matrix style (PWM) model does a surprisingly good job of predicting the distribution of trimming lengths for a variety of V-genes.
source: This one existing analysis (Murugan et al., 2012) has shown that a simple position-weight-matrix style (PWM) model does a surprisingly good job of predicting the distribution of trimming lengths for a variety of V-genes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The 2×4 motif model was replicated using a different, and much larger, repertoire sequencing data set.
source: Using a different, and much larger, repertoire sequencing data set, we have trained this PWM model and replicated previous work (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model had the best model fit and generalizability across different data sets.
source: With this approach, we found that a model containing parameterizations of local sequence context, length, and GC nucleotide content in both directions of the wider sequence (the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model) had the best model fit and generalizability across different data sets (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study shown in Figures 3 and 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model contains 12 parameters compared to 18 parameters in the 2×4 motif model.
source: Despite containing fewer total parameters than the original 2×4 motif model (Murugan et al., 2012) (12 parameters compared to 18 parameters), the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model had better predictive accuracy (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study comparing model parameters and performance.

claim: The magnitude of the negative effects of AT and GC nucleotide counts 3' of the motif are very similar.
source: Interestingly, the magnitude of these negative effects are very similar between AT and GC counts.
evidence: This is an observation from the model coefficients shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The raw number of nucleotides 3' of the motif (e.g. the length) is more important for predicting the trimming probability at a given site compared to the identity of the nucleotides.
source: This suggests that the raw number of nucleotides 3' of the motif (e.g. the length) is more important for predicting the trimming probability at a given site compared to the identity of the nucleotides.
evidence: This is an inference from the similar magnitudes of AT and GC coefficients.

claim: The inferred coefficients from the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model were highly similar between models trained using non-productive V-gene sequences, non-productive J-gene sequences, and productive V-gene sequences.
source: We found that the inferred coefficients were highly similar between the three models (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing models trained on different sequence types shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: The two-side base-count model has the best model fit and generalizability across all held-out groups tested when evaluating models containing only a single feature type.
source: When evaluating models containing only a single feature type, we find that the two-side base-count model which parameterizes GC nucleotide content on both sides of the trimming site (and, indirectly, length) has the best model fit and generalizability across all held-out groups tested (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: GC-content features, which are likely parameterizing the capacity for the sequence to breathe, are more predictive of V-gene trimming probabilities than local sequence context or DNA-shape alone.
source: As such, these GC-content features, which are likely parameterizing the capacity for the sequence to breathe, are more predictive of V-gene trimming probabilities than local sequence context or DNA-shape alone.
evidence: This is an inference from the model comparison results and the known relationship between GC content and DNA breathing.

claim: The inferred trimming profiles for genes with large RMSE improvement still had very low prediction error despite the genes not being included in the model training data set.
source: In fact, we found that the inferred trimming profiles for these genes still had very low prediction error despite the genes not being included in the model training data set (Figure 5B and C), showing the generalizability of these features.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The motif signal may represent a gene-segment-wide sequence motif that appears to get preferentially trimmed, independent of GC-content-related effects.
source: As such, both of these experiments provided evidence that the motif signal may actually represent a gene-segment-wide sequence motif that appears to get preferentially trimmed, independent of GC-content-related effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A set of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the gene encoding the Artemis protein are associated with increasing the extent of V- and J-gene trimming.
source: Using a subset of the V-gene training data set used here, we previously identified a set of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the gene encoding the Artemis protein that are associated with increasing the extent of V- and J-gene trimming (Russell et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Several of the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model coefficients varied significantly in the context of the Artemis-locus SNP rs41298872.
source: Using these methods, we found that several of the 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model coefficients varied significantly in the context of the Artemis-locus SNP rs41298872 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the SNP interaction analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model has high predictive accuracy for both non-productive V- and J-gene sequences from the TCRβ testing data set.
source: We found that the model has high predictive accuracy (i.e. low expected per-sequence conditional log loss) for both non-productive V- and J-gene sequences from the TCRβ testing data set (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model extends well to non-productive V- and J-gene sequences from the TCRα and TCRγ testing data sets.
source: The model also extends well to non-productive V- and J-gene sequences from the TCRα and TCRγ testing data sets and to non-productive V-gene sequences from the IGH testing data set.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model extends well to non-productive V-gene sequences from the IGH testing data set.
source: The model also extends well to non-productive V- and J-gene sequences from the TCRα and TCRγ testing data sets and to non-productive V-gene sequences from the IGH testing data set.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The 1×2 motif + two-side base-count beyond model has relatively poor predictive accuracy for non-productive IGH J-gene sequences.
source: The model has relatively poor predictive accuracy for non-productive IGH J-gene sequences, however.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The two-side base-count beyond terms were dominant compared to the 1×2 motif terms for every data set.
source: With this approach, we found that the two-side base-count beyond terms were dominant compared to the 1×2 motif terms for every data set (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The scale coefficient for the 1×2 motif terms was very small for several of the data sets, especially the IGH data set, indicating only a weak motif-related signal.
source: The scale coefficient for the 1×2 motif terms was very small for several of the data sets, especially the IGH data set, indicating only a weak motif-related signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Sequence motifs that lead to a large increase in trimming probabilities in the model appear at relatively low frequencies within the germline IGH genes.
source: The sequence motifs that lead to a large increase in trimming probabilities in the model appear at relatively low frequencies within the germline IGH genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), perhaps explaining the weakness of the motif-related signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Trimming probabilities are highest for DNA positions near the end of the sequence that contain high GC content upstream.
source: Our results show that trimming probabilities are highest for DNA positions near the end of the sequence that contain high GC content upstream, quantifying the role of sequence-breathing dynamics in the trimming process.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on the model results.

claim: The model quantifies the role of sequence-breathing dynamics in the trimming process.
source: Our results show that trimming probabilities are highest for DNA positions near the end of the sequence that contain high GC content upstream, quantifying the role of sequence-breathing dynamics in the trimming process.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study based on the model results.

claim: The results support a universal, sequence-based trimming mechanism underlying variation across TR and IG loci in humans.
source: Here, our results support a universal, sequence-based trimming mechanism underlying this variation across TR and IG loci in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the validation analysis showing the model extends to multiple loci.

claim: For all TR and IG loci tested, length and GC nucleotide content are relatively more important than local sequence context terms for making accurate model predictions.
source: For all of these loci, we find that length and GC nucleotide content are relatively more important than local sequence context terms for making accurate model predictions.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Many trimming events occur further into the double-stranded gene sequence beyond the single-stranded overhang created during hairpin-opening.
source: While the single-stranded overhang created during hairpin-opening may create a natural single-stranded-to-double-stranded DNA substrate for Artemis binding near the end of the gene sequence, we find that many trimming events occur further into the double-stranded gene sequence.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: DNA positions with fewer double-stranded nucleotides on the 3'-side of the trimming site may have more capacity for sequence-breathing.
source: Because these DNA positions have fewer double-stranded nucleotides on the 3'-side of the trimming site, they may have more capacity for sequence-breathing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results and knowledge of DNA breathing dynamics.

claim: Having a larger number of G-C nucleotides 5' of the trimming site, and perhaps less sequence-breathing capacity, increases the trimming probability.
source: On the 5'-side of the trimming site, we find that having a larger number of G-C nucleotides, and perhaps less sequence-breathing capacity, increases the trimming probability.
evidence: This is a finding from the model coefficients shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The breathing transition can create a transient single-stranded-to-double-stranded DNA substrate that is suitable for Artemis to bind and trim.
source: Perhaps this breathing transition can create a transient single-stranded-to-double-stranded DNA substrate that is suitable for Artemis to bind and trim.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model results.

claim: The finding quantifies sequence-breathing effects that were previously identified through in vitro DNA nuclease assay studies involving Artemis.
source: As such, this finding quantifies sequence-breathing effects that were previously identified through in vitro DNA nuclease assay studies involving Artemis (Chang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion connecting the current findings to previous work.

claim: The observed sequence motif may be serving as a proxy for DNA structure induced by the motif.
source: This suggests that either (1) Artemis actually does possess some ability to recognize specific nucleotides, (2) the observed sequence motif is serving as a proxy for DNA structure induced by the motif, or (3) another nuclease, in addition to Artemis, is responsible for the sequence-specific trimming we observe.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the motif findings.

claim: Another nuclease, in addition to Artemis, may be responsible for the sequence-specific trimming observed.
source: This suggests that either (1) Artemis actually does possess some ability to recognize specific nucleotides, (2) the observed sequence motif is serving as a proxy for DNA structure induced by the motif, or (3) another nuclease, in addition to Artemis, is responsible for the sequence-specific trimming we observe.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the motif findings.

claim: The strength of the sequence motif signal varied across receptor loci.
source: However, because the strength of this sequence motif signal varied across receptor loci, further work will be required to explore its mechanistic basis and presence.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Individuals homozygous (or heterozygous) for rs41298872 may be more capable of trimming at positions that have a larger number of double-stranded nucleotides 3' of the trimming site, especially if the additional nucleotides are AT bases.
source: This suggests that individuals homozygous (or heterozygous) for rs41298872 may be more capable of trimming at positions that have a larger number of double-stranded nucleotides 3' of the trimming site, especially if the additional nucleotides are AT bases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SNP interaction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: If there is more Artemis available, then trimming at less optimal positions (i.e. positions further into the sequence which have less breathing) may be possible.
source: This may be possible if, for example, rs41298872 increases Artemis expression. If there is more Artemis available, then trimming at less optimal positions (i.e. positions further into the sequence which have less breathing) may be possible.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the SNP interaction results.

claim: Individuals homozygous (or heterozygous) for rs41298872 may trim in a less motif-dependent fashion, and are instead more reliant on sequence openness 3' of the trimming site.
source: This may suggest that individuals homozygous (or heterozygous) for rs41298872 may trim in a less motif-dependent fashion, and are instead more reliant on sequence openness 3' of the trimming site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SNP interaction results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Non-productive sequences do not generate proteins that undergo functional selection in the thymus.
source: Non-productive sequences do not generate proteins that undergo functional selection in the thymus, and their recombination statistics should reflect only the V(D)J recombination generation process (Robins et al., 2010; Murugan et al., 2012; Sethna et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The recombination statistics of productive sequences should reflect both V(D)J recombination generation and functional selection.
source: In contrast, the recombination statistics of productive sequences should reflect both V(D)J recombination generation and functional selection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about productive vs non-productive sequences.

claim: The extent of nucleotide trimming varies substantially from gene to gene.
source: The extent of nucleotide trimming varies substantially from gene to gene (Nadel and Feeney, 1995; Nadel and Feeney, 1997; Jackson et al., 2004; Murugan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The 2×4 motif model leverages a 'trimming motif' containing 2 nucleotides 5' of the trimming site and 4 nucleotides 3' of the trimming site to predict the probability of trimming at a given site.
source: Specifically, this model leverages a 'trimming motif' containing 2 nucleotides 5' of the trimming site and 4 nucleotides 3' of the trimming site to predict the probability of trimming at a given site.
evidence: This is a description of the previous model from Murugan et al., 2012.

claim: The 2×4 motif model was designed and trained using sequencing data from just nine individuals.
source: It was designed and trained using sequencing data from just nine individuals (Murugan et al., 2012), and has surprisingly good model fit and predictive accuracy across many V-genes despite its simplicity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TCRβ repertoire sequence data for 666 healthy bone marrow donor subjects was downloaded from the Adaptive Biotechnologies immuneACCESS database.
source: TCRβ repertoire sequence data for 666 healthy bone marrow donor subjects was downloaded from the Adaptive Biotechnologies immuneACCESS database using the link provided in the original publication (Emerson et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the data source for the training data set.

claim: V(D)J recombination scenarios were assigned to each sequence using the IGoR software.
source: V(D)J recombination scenarios were assigned to each sequence from each individual using the IGoR software which is designed to learn unbiased V(D)J recombination statistics from immune sequence reads (Marcou et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the sequence annotation method used.

claim: After processing and filtering steps, V-gene trimming length distributions from 21,193,153 non-productive sequences were used for all model training.
source: After these processing and filtering steps, we used V-gene trimming length distributions from 21,193,153 non-productive sequences for all model training.
evidence: This describes the size of the training data set.

claim: Annotated TCRα and TCRβ repertoire sequence data for 150 healthy subjects was downloaded from a previous publication.
source: Annotated TCRα and TCRβ repertoire sequence data for 150 healthy subjects was downloaded using the link provided in the original publication (Russell et al., 2022b).
evidence: This describes the data source for one of the testing data sets.

claim: Annotated TCRγ repertoire sequence data for 23 healthy bone marrow donor subjects was downloaded from the Adaptive Biotechnologies immuneACCESS database.
source: Annotated TCRγ repertoire sequence data for 23 healthy bone marrow donor subjects was downloaded from the Adaptive Biotechnologies immuneACCESS database (Robins and Pearson, 2015).
evidence: This describes the data source for one of the testing data sets.

claim: Annotated IgG class non-productive IGH repertoire sequence data for nine healthy subjects was obtained from the authors of a previous publication.
source: Annotated IgG class non-productive IGH repertoire sequence data for nine healthy subjects was obtained from the authors of a previous publication (Spisak et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data source for one of the testing data sets.

claim: Productive IGH repertoire sequence data for four healthy subjects was downloaded from a previous publication and the sequences were annotated using partis.
source: Likewise, productive IGH repertoire sequence data for four healthy subjects was downloaded using the link provided in the original publication (Jaffe et al., 2022) and the sequences were annotated using partis (version 0.16.0) (Ralph and Matsen, 2016).
evidence: This describes the data source and annotation method for one of the testing data sets.

claim: Genome-wide SNP array data corresponding to 611 of the training data set individuals was downloaded from The database of Genotypes and Phenotypes.
source: Genome-wide SNP array data corresponding to 611 of the training data set individuals was downloaded from The database of Genotypes and Phenotypes (accession number: phs001918).
evidence: This describes the data source for the SNP data.
